newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian labour force data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian labour force data.

text.p: Australian employment fell 7,200 in February, and the unemployment rate was 8.8 percent, official figures show.
Full-time employment fell 24,200 in the month.
Economists' median forecasts had centred on jobs growth of 10,000 and an unemployment rate of 8.6 percent.
Seperate data showed that housing finance approvals rose 5.0 percent in January. Forecasts had centred on a 4.0 percent rise.
A selection of economists immediate reactions to the data follow:
MICHAEL BLYTHE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK

"The housing recovery is obviously on track, so I don't think there was anything particularly surprising there. I suppose the employment numbers were a little bit surprising given most other recent numbers have come in at the strong end of expectations. I think it probably serves as a bit of a reminder that while another rate cut doesn't appear to be on the agenda at the moment, the rate rise that financial markets seem to have factored in isn't all that close either."
KAREN PRINGLE, TREASURY ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"They are not entirely unexpected. In general because we had had four successive monthly, quite strong, gains we thought it was probably time for some kind of correction in the numbers. Notwithstanding the fact that we still think are signs that the labour market is turning, the employment series did seem to be overstating the extent of the improvement. That (the fall in full-time employment) is consistent with the patterns that we have been seeing in recent months, and I think it tells us that the extent of the improvement in the labour market is not nearly as strong as it looks."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT UBS AUSTRALIA

"At some point we were due to get a pullback on the employment side. It is a lagging indicator, so it would have been remarkable if employment had continued rising very strongly. But the leading edge, housing finance, is still steaming along. So it suggests that there is softness in employment for the time being, but it may not persist as we run through the later part of the year. It certainly means that there is going to be a very long hold before the Reserve Bank does anything with cash rates. There is no pressure on them to think in terms of a pre-emptive tightening."
GLENN MAGUIRE, ECONOMIST, SOCIETE GENERALE AUSTRALIA

"The most worrisome aspect of it is the large fall in male full-time employment. We're still seeing employment being driven by part-time employment at this stage. Due to the higher wages on average commanded, male full-time employment is a better guide to the levels of underlying demand in the economy, and that still remains quite weak. The economy is still well positioned for recovery, but the labour market will be a lagging indicator of how the economy is doing. You won't see any sustainable pick up in employment, or a sustainable drop in the unemployment rate, until the second half of 1997.
